title: Dante (1320)
hookLine: a journey through hell, purgatory and paradise, ending in the love that moves the sun and the other stars
carry: the love that moves the sun

lines: IN THE MIDDLE OF THE ROAD OF OUR LIFE.
cards: A man wakes up lost. He's in the middle of his life, in a dark forest, and he can't say how he got there; the straight road is gone.
That's how the poem opens, in Italian: nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita, in the middle of the road of our life.
The man is the poet himself, Dante Alighieri of Florence, and before he finds his way out he will walk down through hell, climb a mountain, and rise through the heavens.

teach.h: DOWN, UP, AND THROUGH THE HEAVENS.
teach.b: First, the journey. The poem we call the Divine Comedy comes in three parts. In the Inferno, the Roman poet Virgil leads Dante down through hell, where souls are fixed in the choices they refused to let go of.

In the Purgatorio, they climb a mountain where souls are being healed and made ready for God, singing as they go. In the Paradiso, Beatrice, a Florentine woman Dante had loved, guides him up through the heavens.
Second, a detail hiding in plain sight.

teach.h: EVERY PART ENDS ON THE STARS.
teach.b: Each part ends on the same word: stars. Hell ends as they climb out to see the stars again. Purgatory ends with Dante pure and ready to rise to the stars.
And Paradise ends with l'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle, the love that moves the sun and the other stars. Third, that last line.

At the very top, Dante is given a glimpse of God, and he says his words fail him. What's left isn't a speech. It's motion: his desire and his will turning, he says, like a wheel moved evenly by that love.
Finally, why it fits this path.
The first letter of John says, in the Douay-Rheims, "God is charity."

teach.h: THE LOVE THAT MOVES THE SUN.
teach.b: Dante's last line reads like that sentence set in motion. In the poem, the love he finds at the end isn't a feeling in him. It's the thing that turns the sun, and at last turns him.

how: In Italy the Divine Comedy is read in schools and in public readings, including in churches, and popes, among them Benedict XV and Francis, have written in praise of Dante as a Christian poet.

o: the poet who walked from a dark wood to paradise
the Roman poet who guides souls through hell
a Florentine pope who wrote a poem about hell

p: stars, the last word of each part

s: each part of the Divine Comedy ends on the word stars
hell, purgatory and paradise all close on stelle.
Dante's guide through paradise is Virgil
Virgil guides him through hell and up the mountain; Beatrice guides him through the heavens.
at the top of heaven, Dante describes God in a long speech
he says his words fail him. what's left is a will turned like a wheel by love.

games.q: you're Dante, at the top of heaven, given a glimpse of God. you're a poet. what do you do with it?
o: admit your words fail, and tell what love did to you.
stop writing and leave the poem unfinished.
games.why: he says his words fail him, and ends with his desire and will turned like a wheel by the love that moves the sun and the other stars.

practice: Close your eyes and picture the dark first, the way Dante's poem starts, then the first star coming out, and breathe slowly between dark and light.
If you pray, hold the line God is charity; if not, hold the poem's last words, the love that moves the sun and the other stars, and let them be a question.

wordCard.voice: Dante. The Florentine poet who walked, in verse, from a dark wood to the love that moves the sun and the other stars. Today's word.

orig.s: l'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle
orig.say: lah-MOR keh MOH-veh eel SOH-leh eh LAHL-treh STEL-leh
orig.note: Italian, written in the Latin alphabet: the last line of the Paradiso, 'the love that moves the sun and the other stars.'

carryVoice: Your line: the love that moves the sun. Even through city haze, a star is only a short look away. Eight hundred twenty days now.
